title: LumenBridge x Redwood - Solution alignment + quantization tradeoffs

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-10-21
Start: 13:00 PT
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Sofia Ruiz (Redwood SE), Daniel Kim (CTO - LumenBridge), Priya Rao (Platform Eng Manager - LumenBridge), Evan Holt (Security - LumenBridge), Rita Alvarez (SWE - LumenBridge)

Summary: Quick recap at top: discuss packaging for marketplace listing, private/VPC deployment patterns, quantization tradeoffs for their low-latency summarization service, and security gating items.

---Transcript---
[00:00:06] Jordan (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we'll do a quick agenda. I'm Jordan, AE. We've got Maya and Sofia from the SE team. Daniel, Priya, Evan, Rita, great to have you.
[00:00:18] Daniel (LumenBridge): Thanks, Jordan. On our side the main thing is we want to understand how Redwood's packaging and listing will map to our on-prem edge clusters and also the hosted flows. Cost and latency are huge.
[00:00:30] Maya (Redwood SE): Great. We'll walk through two patterns: 1) Marketplace listing for quick onboarding to a hosted instance, and 2) the private/VPC package with Helm chart for on-prem or cloud VPC installs. We'll also show the quantized benchmarks we ran last week.
[00:00:45] Priya: Quick note — our real-time summarizer is about 20 QPS per node, 300ms p95 target. We need a plan that doesn't blow up cost.
[00:00:55] Sofia: Understood. Our batching and prefix cache options usually let you hit that without full fp32.
[00:01:10] [00:01:10] Jordan: Quick housekeeping — we'll add links in chat to the packaging checklist and the sample helm repo. Jordan posts: https://redwood.example.com/partner-packaging/lumenbridge-v1.pdf and git.redwood.com/partners/lumenbridge/helm.
[00:01:25] Rita (LumenBridge): I clicked the link, looks good. One immediate question — what quantization recipes do you support in the private deploy? Is it 8-bit, 4-bit, or 3-bit?
[00:01:36] Maya: We commonly support int8, 4-bit (GPTQ-style) and some experimental 3-bit for certain Llama-family variants. Caveat: the 3-bit paths are model-specific and can introduce hallucination modes in long contexts. We recommend running eval sets.
[00:01:51] Daniel: Right, accuracy drift is our biggest fear. Our summaries need to preserve entities and dates.
[00:01:57] Maya: Absolutely. In the benchmarks I ran with LumenBridge's sample workload we saw token-level ROUGE degradation of ~1.8% at 4-bit, and latency improvement of about 2.4x on A100-like blades. But that number varies with sequence length and kv/cache hit rates.
[00:02:17] [00:02:17] Sofia: Also worth noting that our runtime can do mixed-precision where KV cache stays higher-precision to avoid degradation on long threads. It's a knob in the deployment manifest.
[00:02:30] Evan (Security): On KMS and key management: in private deployments we need HSM-backed keys and audit exports. Do you write audit logs to S3/Blob? How granular are they?
[00:02:42] Maya: For Private, we integrate with customer KMS via CMK or HSM, and audit events stream to an output you configure — we support S3, Azure Blob, or syslog. Events include model load, key access, and API-level request IDs. Retention is up to the customer. We'll share the audit event schema.
[00:02:59] Priya: Can you include model checksum and kernel selection in logs? We need for reproducibility.
[00:03:05] Sofia: Yes, we log model sha, quant profile, kernel version, and the shader/kern label — sometimes transcribed as uh kernel version in the logs.
[00:03:13] [00:03:13] Jordan: Quick pause — there's an earlier marketplace preflight checklist that shows required metadata: listing name, versions, billing SKU, trial credits, and the sample app integration.
[00:03:25] Daniel: On the marketplace side, our procurement team prefers a private listing where our infra team can provision a Dedicated capacity but still buy through marketplace billing. Is that supported?
[00:03:37] Maya: Yes, we support marketplace-linked dedicated offers. The packaging requires an ops bundle that includes the helm chart, a manifest with SKU mapping, and support SLA level. We'll send an example.
[00:03:49] Rita: Are there differences in networking? We run in a restricted VPC with egress limits. How does the private control plane behave?
[00:03:57] Maya: In private mode the control plane can be hosted with a VPC-peering model or you can opt for the self-hosted control plane inside your VPC. The former needs minimal egress for heartbeats; the latter is fully air-gapped except for licensing calls if you enable them.
[00:04:14] Evan: Licensing calls are a non-starter unless they can go through our proxy. We need full RBAC and SSO/SAML for admin.
[00:04:22] Jordan: We do SAML and OIDC. Admin RBAC and teams are supported via SCIM sync. We'll put the SSO doc link in follow-up.
[00:04:31] [00:04:31] Priya: Back to perf — what about kernel selection? Our sequences vary a lot. Sometimes short single-sentence summaries, sometimes 2k tokens.
[00:04:40] Maya: The runtime picks kernels based on sequence-length histogram. For very short sequences we favor low-latency kernels with fused attention, for longer it picks kernel variants optimized for memory throughput. If you pin a particular run level, you can override kernel selection but we don't recommend it for mixed workloads.
[00:04:59] Daniel: If we go quantized 4-bit, are we blocked from switching to 8-bit or fp16 at runtime?
[00:05:05] Sofia: You can run model variants side-by-side. The smart router will failover to a fp16 variant if a quantized variant crosses an error threshold. That is used in production in fallbacks for critical paths.
[00:05:18] [00:05:18] Rita: Any known issues with beam search/Top-k sampling after quantization? We use nucleus sampling for summaries and sometimes beam for extractive pieces.
[00:05:27] Maya: Sampling is generally fine, but beam search can magnify small logits errors introduced by aggressive quant. We recommend running beam width sanity checks and calibrating temperature. We'll include sampling profiles in the benchmark CSV.
[00:05:41] Jordan: Quick interjection — competitors like CloudAI advertise black-box endpoints but less observability. This is a good differentiator for Redwood — we give trace-level data per request.
[00:05:52] Daniel: That's helpful. If we can get request-level token cost and latency per route we can do chargeback internally.
[00:05:59] Sofia: Console supports token-level breakdown and per-model dashboards. That is included in Dedicated/Private.
[00:06:08] [00:06:08] Maya: I'll walk through the microbenchmark table I ran. (screen share) For LumenBridge sample 512-token context: fp32 p95 ~420ms on baseline node, 4-bit p95 ~170ms, int8 p95 ~220ms. Quality deltas: fp32 -> 4-bit BLEU/ROUGE slight drop but entity preservation was mostly stable for this workload.
[00:06:30] Priya: Do you have the raw CSV? We want to import into our perf dashboard.
[00:06:34] Maya: Yes, I'll post the raw CSV to the shared folder. Link: https://redwood-artifacts.example.com/lumenbridge/benchmarks/2027-10-21.csv
[00:06:42] [00:06:42] Jordan: Another note — packaging needs a small reference app that demonstrates auth and webhooks for streaming responses. For marketplace listing the sample app must pass the quickstart flow.
[00:06:55] Daniel: For on-prem we'll use our existing helm operator. Does Redwood's chart play nicely with our operator?
[00:07:02] Sofia: We provide a standard Helm chart and an umbrella chart to integrate into upstream operators. Our chart exposes a few hooks for init containers that configure KV cache volumes.
[00:07:13] Rita: What about local NVDISK and node selectors for GPU types? We have mixed clusters.
[00:07:19] Maya: Chart supports nodeSelector, tolerations, and a device-plugin annotation for GPU SKU. We recommend using our instance labeling scheme so the model scheduler can pick appropriate nodes.
[00:07:31] [00:07:31] Evan: Security follow-up — can we enable audit events for model prompt inputs? We have PII concerns and only want metadata for audit, not full prompts stored.
[00:07:42] Sofia: Yes, there is a redact option and sampling. You can redact prompt content at ingestion and still capture request ids, token counts, and model variant. We'll add the redact config to the manifest.
[00:07:53] Priya: How about upgrade windows? We can't take down the fleet for rolling upgrades that are disruptive.
[00:07:59] Maya: We support canary deploys and auto-fallback. The rollout process includes a traffic-shifting policy and automatic rollback on latency/err thresholds. Many customers run blue-green.
[00:08:12] [00:08:12] Jordan: Let's talk deliverables again — we'll share packaging checklist, helm repo, benchmark CSV, and an example marketplace metadata JSON.
[00:08:23] Daniel: Sounds good. One ask — can Redwood run a short spike test on a dedicated dev cluster with our traces to validate latencies?
[00:08:31] Maya: Yes, we can run a pilot. We'll need a limited dataset and a billing/commit agreement for the pilot cluster. Jordan can handle the paperwork.
[00:08:41] Evan: About SOC — we've got a SOC 2 Type II requirement and need to see audit evidence of key rotations. Are rotations automated?
[00:08:50] Sofia: Rotations are supported, and the control plane can report rotation events. We'll include a rotation log and example audit outputs.
[00:08:58] [00:08:58] Jordan: Ok, I think we're getting alignment. Let's capture the decisions: 1) Run 4-bit and int8 microbenchmarks against LumenBridge traces, 2) Redwood to provide helm and marketplace artifacts, 3) Security deep-dive week of 11/1.
[00:09:14] Priya: Agreed. We also want a follow-up to review fallback policies and router configs.
[00:09:20] Jordan: Noted — Maya will own the router config review.
[00:09:24] [00:09:24] Sofia: One more subtlety — if you use prefix/KV caching aggressively, you might see token-cost amortization but cache churn for multi-tenant workloads can increase memory overhead. We'll include recommended cache TTLs per workload profile.
[00:09:39] Daniel: Is there a recommended quantization profile for summarization specifically?
[00:09:44] Maya: For summarization we saw 4-bit with mixed precision KV cache gave the best throughput/cost balance with minimal quality loss. For very high fidelity extractive tasks consider int8 or fp16.
[00:09:58] [00:09:58] Rita: Cool. We'll review the CSV and share PR for helm tweaks.
[00:10:04] Jordan: Great — last minute — competitors. EdgeServe's prepackaged on-prem has lower observability in our experience, CloudAI has sticky pricing. We'll emphasize our traceability.
[00:10:18] Priya: Thanks all.
[00:10:21] [00:10:21] End of meeting notes: rest of transcript contains smaller clarifications and name mixups where automated captions sometimes wrote "kay-vee cash" instead of KV cache. Occasional crosstalk when people had network lag.

Recap (spoken): Jordan: we'll follow up with the packaging checklist and set the security deep-dive. Maya: I'll run the quantization table and post CSV. Priya: provide sample traces and latency targets. Evan: will prepare compliance Qs and KMS diagram.
